question: Are the Qur'anic verses about faces turning white and black on Judgment Day racist?
asked: During these riots and police brutality, Islamophobes in my town in Australia are quoting Qur'an translations that seem to suggest the Qur'an has racist verses, such as Surah Ali Imran verse 106, "on that day some faces will be white and some faces will be black," and Surah Az-Zumar verse 60, "on the Day of Judgment, those who lied against Allah, their faces will be turned black." How do I respond to these allegations?
answer:
The answer to this question: subhanAllah, what a great, egregious translation error, a mistranslation that might even be intentional. We seek Allah's refuge, a'udhu billah. How can anybody, anybody, accuse the Qur'an of being racist? This clearly demonstrates that this person either has an evil intent or, most likely, has no clue what the Arabic actually says.

And the Qur'an, it is true, does mention the words tabyaddu and taswaddu. It is very true. **However, these verb tenses have nothing to do with skin colors. There is no racial element being implied at all.** And anybody who really understands Arabic will understand this. The problem comes that most of the people who translate the Qur'an are not qualified to translate the Qur'an. And I do not even deny that maybe some translator actually said that, and I think it is actually true, I did find it in one translation: "their faces will be whitened," and "their faces will be blackened." A'udhu billah, this is not how the verse should be translated.

Tabyaddu and taswaddu, or muswadda, are linguistic forms that have nothing to do with the color of one's skin, and hence any person who understands Arabic would never associate these verbs with human skin color. These Qur'anic verbs and nouns are in fact associated with the brightness of the day. And the brightness of the day is associated with optimism; it is associated with a new timeframe, a hope. And muswadda or taswaddu is associated with worrying times, or maybe the darkness of the night.

And by the way, those connotations of night and day are found even in the English language. For example, we say "the rise of a new dawn" when we intend optimism. We say "dark, stormy clouds" when we intend something that is terrifying. When we say "the rise of a new dawn," does anybody think of the skin color white? No, it is the sun; it is optimism. So this is the notion of tabyaddu and taswaddu.

And in fact, the Qur'an is actually very explicit. Look at Surah Yunus verse 27, where darkness, the word taswaddu, is explicitly linked to the issue of the night, nothing to do with skin colors. Allah says, qita'an min al-layli muzliman: that it is muzlim, from the night's darkness. So the issue of whiteness and darkness is a huge mistranslation.

Rather, what the Qur'an is describing, when the Qur'an says of the people of Paradise, yawma tabyaddu wujuh, the meaning is that the faces will be optimistic. The faces will be, in English we can say, beaming with joy. That's how it should be translated. Nothing to do with whiteness whatsoever. The noun here has to do with beaming with joy. And then the opposite, taswaddu: they're going to be gloomy with fear, with trepidation. That's what taswaddu means. It has nothing to do, again, with the color of one's skin.

And we all know, alhamdulillah, that white and brown and black, all of these skin colors, alhamdulillah, we know very clearly that they mean nothing for the issue of salvation. It is an established principle of Islam that there is no superiority of a white over a black, of an Arab over a non-Arab, except with taqwa. And so inshaAllah, people of all skin colors, the white of them, the black of them, the brown of them, the yellow of them, every skin color: those that are righteous, they will be tabyaddu wujuh, and those that are not righteous, they will be taswaddu wujuh. So we ask Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala to make all of us, no matter what our skin colors are, of those whose faces are tabyaddu, meaning bright with happiness and glory.
